records.title: Frame Fatigue & Cracking at the Steering-Box Mount
records.description: On Scout IIs the steering gear bolts to a relatively thin section of the boxed frame rail. Decades of steering loads — made far worse by oversized tires — flex that area until the frame fatigues, bends, and finally cracks around the box. Owners first notice it as vague, wandering steering as the box rocks on a softening rail; left alone it can crack the rail outright, which is catastrophic at highway speed. It is one of the best-known Scout II structural failures.
records.solution: The proven fix is a bolt-on steering-box-to-frame brace (the 'Straight Steer' brace and similar reinforcement plates from IH Parts America / Anything Scout, for 1971-80 Scout II/Terra/Traveler). It ties the box to a second frame location, stiffening the rail so it stops flexing — tightening up the wander AND stopping the fatigue cracking. On trucks already cracked, restorers weld in a reinforcement/boxing plate first, then add the brace. Considered mandatory on anything running 33-inch or larger tires.
symptoms: Wandering, vague on-center steering
Visible flexing of the frame at the steering box under load
Hairline or open cracks in the frame rail at the gearbox
Steering box appears to move/rock when wheel is turned

citations.title: IH Parts America — Straight Steer Steering Box Brace, 71-80 Scout II/Terra/Traveler
ScoutParts.com — Scout II Power Steering Box Reinforcement Plate

records.title: Frame, Rocker & Floor Rust — the Scout's Defining Weak Point
records.description: Scouts were never galvanized and left the factory with no body seals or splash shields, so road grime and water pack into every seam. After decades the body literally rusts off the chassis. The structural danger zones are the boxed frame at the rear spring hangers and rear crossmember, the body mounts, the inner rockers, and the floors/cargo (hatch) area. Front fenders, door sills and the windshield/cowl frame trap moisture and hide rot under filler. Frame rot at the rear shackle mounts and crossmember is a 'walk away or full rebuild' problem.
records.solution: Restorers do a body-off (frame-off) restoration: media-blast the frame, cut out and weld in new boxing/crossmember sections, then coat inside and out and inject cavity wax (e.g. Fluid Film / wax-oil) into the boxed rails to stop it returning. Reproduction steel — full floor pans, rocker/rocker-cap panels, cab corners, rear quarters and tailgate skins (Anything Scout, IH Parts America, C2C Fabrication) — replaces rotted shemetal rather than skim-filling it. Reinstall on fresh polyurethane body-mount bushings. Done once properly, the cavity wax + sealed seams is what keeps it from rotting again.
symptoms: Flaking/bubbling paint along rockers and rear quarters
Soft or holed floor pans and cargo floor
Frame perforation at rear spring mounts and crossmember
Doors/tailgate misaligned from frame sag
Crunchy/rotten windshield frame and cowl

citations.title: Buyer's Guide: International Scout II — Top 5 Things to Look Out For
Bulletproof Restorations — International Scout (full frame-off rust remediation)

records.title: Heat-Soaked Starter Solenoid — No Hot-Restart
records.description: After the engine sits hot for ten minutes, the starter-mounted solenoid heat-soaks (it sits right next to the exhaust head pipe) and the truck won't restart — it cranks painfully slow, just clicks, or does nothing, exactly like a flat battery. The root cause is two-fold: heat raising resistance at the solenoid, AND the aging factory ignition switch + harness no longer delivering enough current to the solenoid trigger through worn, oxidized connections.
records.solution: The bulletproof fix restorers use is a remote starter relay kit: a Ford-style or cube relay mounted away from exhaust heat that takes a tiny trigger current from the worn ignition switch and switches full battery current straight to the solenoid (kits from ScoutParts/IH Parts America). This restores strong hot cranking and takes the load off the old switch. Pair it with refreshed/upsized battery and starter cables and re-fit the factory exhaust-to-starter heat shield. Many also fit a modern gear-reduction mini-starter that tolerates heat far better.
symptoms: Engine won't restart when hot but starts fine cold
Solenoid clicks or just one click on hot restart
Slow cranking once warmed up
Returns to normal after the engine cools

citations.title: ScoutParts.com — Starter Relay Kit w/ 12V Harness (more power to the solenoid)
IH Parts America Forum — '80 Scout II won't start when hot

records.title: Holley 'Gold Box' Electronic Ignition High Failure Rate
records.description: Later Scouts use the Holley 'gold box' electronic ignition amplifier mounted on the firewall (right of center). It has a notoriously high failure rate: the module goes intermittent and then dies — sometimes over weeks, sometimes in minutes — leaving the truck dead with no spark. A common tell is black-grey potting compound oozing out of the box. The factory replacement boxes are pricey and fail the same way.
records.solution: Restorers stop chasing replacement gold boxes and convert the distributor to a PerTronix Ignitor (a self-contained magnetic pickup that replaces the points/module entirely) — the forum consensus fix because it costs about the same as a new gold box but is a permanent upgrade, not 'more of the same.' It eliminates the firewall amplifier as a failure point and cures the associated hard-start/stalling gremlins. Owners wanting more output instead drop in a self-contained HEI-style distributor. Either way the fragile gold box leaves the truck.
symptoms: Sudden total loss of spark / no-start
Intermittent stalling and misfire that comes and goes
Black/grey potting material seeping from the firewall box
Engine dies when hot then restarts when cool

citations.title: IH Parts America Forum — Scout II Ignition Issues (gold box failure, PerTronix fix)
Summit Racing — PerTronix Electronic Distributor Conversion Kits, Scout II

records.title: Marginal Cooling System & Frozen Heat-Riser Overheating
records.description: The IH V8s (266/304/345/392) run hot in Scout IIs — the factory radiator and cooling capacity are marginal, especially with A/C, larger tires, or any added power. A specific Scout failure mode is the exhaust heat-riser valve seizing CLOSED: it dams exhaust under the intake, which overheats the engine, drives an over-lean mixture, and in the worst case can start an engine fire. General overheating is one of the most-cited stock-drivetrain complaints.
records.solution: Restorers upgrade to a high-capacity aluminum (or thicker multi-core) radiator and a high-flow water pump, add a proper shroud and a clutch or electric fan, and run a 180-degree thermostat. The seized heat-riser is freed, rebuilt, or deleted/locked open (it's only needed for fast cold-start warm-up). On full builds the chronic-overheat issue is permanently solved by the popular LS V8 swap, which also cures the limited stock power. These fixes turn a temperamental cooler into a reliable one.
symptoms: Temp gauge climbing in traffic or on grades
Boil-over, especially with A/C on
Lean running / spark knock when hot
Heat-riser valve seized solid when checked by hand

citations.title: ScoutParts.com — IH V8 Heat Riser Valve (266/304/345/392) replacement
IH Parts America Forum — Improved Cooling 345

records.title: Rusted/Pinholed Steel Fuel Tank & Failing Sending Unit
records.description: The original steel fuel tanks rust from the inside and develop pinhole leaks; owners chase patches for years with no lasting fix. The internal rust and varnish also clog the fuel system and wreck the float-type sending unit, so the gauge reads stuck on empty/full or erratic, and corroded float arms and worn senders give junk readings — a classic Scout fuel-system headache that also feeds rust/debris into carburetors.
records.solution: Restorers stop patching and fit a modern polyethylene replacement tank (e.g. Raybuck 19-gal poly tank for 72-80 Scout II) — it physically can't rust again — installed with new straps, filler hose, and a fresh sending unit and gasket at the same time (the standard 'do them together' rule). Add an inline filter and, on builds running EFI/LS swaps, an EMS/in-tank pump provision. Result is reliable fuel delivery and an accurate, repaired gauge.
symptoms: Fuel smell / wet spots from tank pinholes
Fuel gauge stuck on empty or full or wildly erratic
Rust/debris clogging filter and carburetor
Tank patches that keep re-leaking

citations.title: Raybuck — 1972-1980 Scout II 19-gallon polyethylene replacement tank
Gas Tank Depot — International Harvester / Scout sending units (stuck/erratic gauge fix)

records.title: Weak Stock Charging System (Low-Output Alternator/Generator)
records.description: Early Scout 80/800s left the factory with a generator, and even alternator-equipped Scout IIs only make about 50-60 amps. That is not enough headroom for a restored truck running modern lighting, a stereo, off-road lights, a winch, or an electric fan — it leaves the battery undercharged, dims the headlights, and causes inoperative reverse/tail lights. Dim lights and taillight/reverse-light failures are common, aging-electrical complaints.
records.solution: The community upgrade is a one-wire/plug-in high-output alternator — a GM CS130 bolts in as a near plug-and-play swap, and 140-160 amp units are sold specifically for Scouts (Anything Scout, IH Parts America). On a Scout 80/800 still running a generator, restorers do the full generator-to-alternator conversion. The critical, often-skipped step: run a new heavy-gauge charge wire from the alternator output to the battery (the original wiring can't carry the higher output). Pair with a refreshed ground strap set to cure the dim-light/dead-light gremlins.
symptoms: Dim or flickering headlights, especially at idle
Battery repeatedly going flat / undercharged
Inoperative reverse and tail lights
Ammeter showing low or no charge

citations.title: Anything Scout — 160-Amp Upgraded Alternator for Scout
IH Parts America Forum — Alternator upgrade (CS130 plug-and-play, heavy charge wire)
